Abstract.AbstractText: This study aimed to determine whether repeated-sprint running with deceleration aggravates markers of muscle damage or delays the recovery of performance compared to repeated-sprint running without deceleration. Fourteen male team-sport athletes performed two randomly ordered testing sessions on a non-motorised treadmill with one session requiring participants to decelerate (TMd) within 4 s before stopping, or immediately step to the side of the treadmill belt at the completion of each sprint (TMa). Peak and mean velocities, speed decrement, blood lactate concentrations and oxygen uptake were monitored during the repeated-sprint running protocols. Countermovement vertical jump (CMJ) performance, perceived muscle soreness, sit-and-reach flexibility, plasma creatine kinase (CK), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and myoglobin (Mb) concentrations were quantified immediately before and after and 45 min, 24 and 48 h after repeated-sprint running protocols. While muscle damage was indicated by increases in CK, LDH, and Mb (p<0.05) in both groups, there was no significant effect of condition (TMa vs. TMd) on any of the measured performance or physiological variables (p>0.05). The present study indicated that the removal of deceleration from repeated-sprint running on a non-motorised treadmill has no effect on metabolism or performance during or after repeated-sprint running, or markers of muscle damage.
